forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 25%. May 6 2026: no new credible AGI declaration since last update. The May 4 Pentagon AI awards (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and 4 others cleared; Anthropic excluded) reinforce that lab-government coordination on any 'AGI achieved' declaration remains fractious. Frontier model cadence stays compressed (Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3-Codex shipped February with major agentic gains; GPT-5.4 1M-token context now live), but no lab CEO has pivoted from 'within a few years' framing to 'achieved.' Industry leader timeline anchors: Amodei 2026–27, Altman 2035, Hassabis 5–10 years, researcher median 2047. Metaculus community estimate ~25% by 2029. ~43 months to resolution.
forecasts.base_rate: ~25% aggregated from Metaculus, Kalshi and expert surveys for AGI by 2029
factors_up: Frontier release cadence remains compressed in 2026 YTD (+1pp)
Amodei continues to anchor 2026-27 AGI timeline (+1pp)
GPT-5.4 with 1M-token context demonstrates agentic capability (+1pp)
Pentagon awarded contracts to 8 frontier firms — capability validation (+1pp)
factors_down: AGI definition still contested across labs and academia (-3pp)
Resolution window narrowing to <44 months (-2pp)
Hassabis publicly anchoring 5–10 year human-level AGI timeline (-1pp)
Lab-government friction (Anthropic Pentagon exclusion) raises coordination risk for declaration (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: What threshold will the first lab use to claim AGI?
Whether competitive pressure forces an early declaration before consensus forms
How regulators / governments respond to a lab-led declaration
update_triggers: Any frontier lab issues a formal AGI declaration
≥3 leading AI researchers publicly state AGI achieved
Major capability jump on ARC-AGI-2 / Humanity's Last Exam (>15pp single-release)

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 20%. McKinsey is now telegraphing ~10% workforce cut over the next two years (already shed ~10% in past 18 months); PwC cut 1,500 US jobs; EY delayed new-hire start dates. Trajectory is consistent with 15-25% peak-to-trough employment decline by 2030, but the 33% threshold remains demanding because (a) consultancy revenue is still growing in absolute terms at most firms (BCG +10% in 2024), (b) the cuts are concentrated in support/back-office roles less directly tied to client revenue, and (c) the question requires '2+ credible analyses' attributing decline primarily to AI — current narrative blends AI with cyclical demand and pyramid-model exhaustion. Latest signal: Fast Company / Inc / The Logic now consistently framing this as 'AI reckoning' rather than cyclical, raising attribution probability.
forecasts.base_rate: ~10% historical base rate for any service sector to lose >30% in 5 years from a single technology shock
factors_up: McKinsey plans 10% workforce reduction over 2 years (+3pp)
PwC, EY, Deloitte, KPMG all making AI-attributed cuts (+2pp)
Media narrative consolidating around 'AI reckoning' framing (+1pp)
Pyramid model under structural threat from Lilli/Deckster-class tools (+1pp)
factors_down: BCG revenue still +10% YoY in 2024 (-2pp)
33% is a high threshold — requires near-collapse, not gradual decline (-3pp)
Consultancies pivoting to AI implementation services as new revenue line (-2pp)
Resolution requires '2+ credible analyses' attributing primarily to AI (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether Big 4 audit/tax can offset consulting decline at parent level
Whether AI implementation revenue replaces lost strategy revenue
How analysts will attribute decline (cyclical vs structural vs AI)
update_triggers: Any MBB or Big 4 firm announces revenue decline of >15% YoY
Headcount falls below 2024 baseline by >20% at major firms
Bain or BCG follows McKinsey with public 10%+ cuts

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 3% on the eve of May 7 2026 local elections. Latest polling: Reform UK ~27%, Conservatives ~18.3%, Labour ~18-19%, Greens ~14.3%. Reform projected to gain 1,300+ council seats and take Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk councils; Labour projected to lose 1,500-1,900 councillors from a low base. ITV London poll (May 5) shows Labour 'under siege' even in capital. With ~3.5 years to GE deadline (Dec 2029) and Reform consistently 7-9pp clear of Labour, the path to Labour-as-largest-party requires either (a) Reform collapse, (b) major Labour leadership change with rebound, or (c) Reform-Conservative coalition fracture. None visible at present.
forecasts.base_rate: ~15% reference class for incumbent UK governing party falling >10pp in polls and recovering to win most seats within a single term
factors_up: Reform vote share could fragment if it splinters or loses leadership focus (+1pp)
Labour incumbency advantage in marginal seats (+1pp)
3.5 years is long enough for mean reversion in polls (+1pp)

Starmer popularity at record low — leadership challenge possible but no rebound evidence (-1pp)

Whether Labour replaces Starmer and pivots messaging
How Reform-Conservative voter overlap resolves at GE under FPTP

Labour leadership change

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 1%. The April 2026 BoE Monetary Policy Report (released April 30) projects CPI at 3.1% in 2026 Q2, rising to 3.3% in Q3 and rising further in Q4 — a 1.4pp upward revision from February's 2.0% Q3 projection. Bank Rate held at 3.75% (April 29 8-1 vote, with one member voting to hike). With <8 months until the Jan 2027 deadline and CPI rising rather than falling, the path to a sub-2.0% monthly print would require an unprecedented disinflationary shock (sudden energy collapse, sharp sterling spike, abrupt demand crash). No such catalyst is in the OBR or BoE projection set.
forecasts.base_rate: ~5% reference class for CPI dropping >1.5pp in a single quarter absent a recession
factors_up: Energy prices could collapse on Middle East de-escalation or supply surge (+1pp)
Possible sharp sterling appreciation if Reform government rumours intensify (+0pp)
factors_down: BoE projection 3.1% Q2 → 3.3% Q3 → higher Q4 — wrong direction (-3pp)
BoE 8-1 hold vote with hawkish dissent — no near-term cuts (-1pp)
<8 months remain to deadline (-1pp)
OBR March 2026 EFO consistent with above-target inflation through 2027 (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether energy base effects produce a single low print in late 2026
Whether a sudden recession compresses inflation rapidly
Whether ONS CPI methodology revisions affect monthly print
update_triggers: Any monthly CPI print of 2.5% or lower
Brent oil drop below $55 sustained for 4+ weeks
BoE explicit guidance toward sub-2% Q3-Q4 2026 print

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 42%. OBR March 2026 EFO confirms real GDP per person growth at 1.1% average 2026–2030 with productivity (TFP) growth picking up to 1% in the medium term. Adding ~0.5% from labour-supply growth declining toward 0.5% by 2030, headline real GDP growth lands close to 1.5–1.6% over the late 2020s baseline. For the 2030–2039 mean to exceed 1.5%, productivity has to keep pace with OBR's medium-term path AND labour supply must hold up against demographic ageing. AI-led upside scenario (1.5%+ productivity) brackets the 'yes' outcome; downside scenario (0.5% productivity, post-GFC average) sits well below 1.5%. With a Reform-leaning political trajectory now likely (per May 7 polling), policy mix on planning, immigration and EU trade is uncertain — could go either way for productivity.
forecasts.base_rate: ~35% reference class for UK delivering decade-average >1.5% real GDP growth in a post-2010 productivity environment
factors_up: OBR medium-term TFP picks up to 1.0% (+2pp)
AI productivity dividend if scaling holds through 2030 (+2pp)
Late-2020s baseline tracking close to 1.5-1.6% headline (+1pp)
factors_down: Labour supply growth declining toward 0.5% by 2030 (-2pp)
Political flux (Reform path) risks planning/immigration/EU policy reversals (-2pp)
Demographic ageing intensifies in 2030s (-2pp)
Climate transition costs likely to weigh on near-decade output (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether AI productivity dividend materialises in UK output statistics
Whether net migration policy reverses post-2030
Whether planning reform delivers material housing-led productivity gain
update_triggers: OBR multi-year TFP downgrade below 0.7%
